catalog_quote: XII. 4. Stress. Stress in Awankari is prominent. ... Stress is mostly a matter of intonation and will be discussed as such later. But here some broad features of the incidence of stress may be mentioned. XII. 4 i. Disyllabic words (1) When a long or half-long vowel occurs finally in both syllables, stress is even ... (2) When the two syllables are short, stress is again even. ... (3) When the first syllable is long and the second short, there is slight stress on the first ... (4) There is prominent stress on the final syllable when it is long, preceded by a short syllable, i'mán, faith ... o'gás, sky ... EXCEPTIONS. Variation in stress is due to expressiveness. Exception to No. (4) occurs in Past participles and a number of loanwords. ... Similarly exceptions to No. (2) occur in a number of abstract nouns and some verbal forms ... tone_statements.quote: XI. 4. i. Tones A tone effects an important semantic difference in the language. Compare— mal, property ma‘l, rope va, wind va’, plough (v.) [...] The principal types of tones applicable to syllables in Awankari are the following : (1) The falling tone. The larynx rises very slightly at the primary articulation of the tone and then falls down below its normal position. It is represented by the sign [‘] in this thesis, as in ba*r, outside mo‘ro’, first veld, vacant gha’, grass. This tone is most common in Awankari and more prominent in it than in any Lahndi dialect. Itisa particular feature of Wanddhi, less so of PAkhri, and least of Reshi. (2) The high tone. The larynx rises quickly and falls slowly in the articulation of this tone. In fact it isa variety of the tone No. (1). The same syllables of Wanddhi having falling tone are pronounced in Reshi with the high tone
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Awankari Lahndi: lexical tone of the Punjabi type but with voiced aspirates retained; a high-falling tone (Wanadhi) ~ high(-rising) tone (Reshi) on the same lexical items, a marginal low-rising tone in a dozen words, toneless syllables otherwise; high-toned syllables always carry stress.

sources.quote: Historical volume; says the Awankari stress system is simple and stress 'exceptionally strong' (Pakhri sub-dialect 'stress is very strong', causes consonant doubling), that Awankari 'has normally preserved Sanskrit stress-accent' with exceptions, and refers the synchronic description to Lahndi Phonetics and to its own accent chapter. Nothing that alters the penult / disyllable-by-length coding.
sources.locator: Introduction (dialect features (5)-(6)), sec. I.5 'Stress' (the scanned text)

tone.summary: Awankari Lahndi: contrastive word tone from loss of non-initial h/voiced aspiration — a very frequent high-falling tone plus a (low-)rising tone, realised falling in Wanadhi vs rising in Reshi; initial voiced aspirates preserved (unlike Punjabi); simple regular stress.

sources.quote: No word-stress placement rule stated; only incidental references to 'post-accentual closed syllables' (epenthetic -o- generalized there in Ko./Pe.) and 'accented diphthongs in monosyllables'. Confirms identity and authority: Avankari (Av.) is a member of 'Hindko proper' with Ghebi, Attock-Haripur and Kohat Hindko; Bahri's Lahndi Phonology (1962) and Lahndi Phonetics (1963) 'are studies of outstanding quality' and the LSI description 'has been completely superseded by the excellent material presented by Bahri'.

sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog lahn1241). Southern Lahndi dialects have one rising tone (starts low, rises considerably, falls a little) contrasting with a level tone; the northern dialect Awankari additionally has a second rising-tone variant (starts mid, rises slightly, falls below mid), both combining phonologically with the level tone, and 'a small group of words in Awankari also has a falling tone'; details deferred to the Phonetics section (not in the excerpt). No verbatim quote recorded because a tone statement is already listed here.
